cases.evidence: seg_trans adds hallucinated 'so I took it' not present in reference
cases.cause: clause ends in a dependent connective (-가지고) that needs the prior clause's cause; isolating it made the translator invent a filler action
cases.proposed_rule: Do not place a boundary immediately before a clause whose only verb ending is a dependent connective (e.g. -가지고, -아서) that encodes cause/result tied to the previous clause; keep it attached or move the tag earlier.

cases.cause: the subject pronoun implicit in the first clause was not carried into the second segment, so the second piece lost its referent

example_pair.input: 아니 근데 우리도 부담되는데 너무 먹고 싶어서 어쩔 수 없었다고 그래가지고 먹고 맛있게 먹었어.

cases.proposed_rule: If the subject of a clause is stated only after the proposed boundary, move the boundary after the subject introduction instead of before it.

example_pair.input: 그리고 이제 작년에 이제 3개월 이제 노력을 해서 이제 편입을 준비하게 되었는데 혹시 군대 전역하고

cases.cause: a cluster of filler interjections was left attached to the main clause instead of being split off as its own fast segment
cases.proposed_rule: When a segment begins with a cluster of filler interjections (아, 어, 근데) before the real clause, split them into their own piece.

example_pair.input: 왜? 아 어 근데 그거 안 먹으면 그 안 나와.
example_pair.output: 왜? <SEG> 아 어 근데 <SEG> 그거 안 먹으면 그 안 나와.

summary: The main failure mode is under-segmentation: long or filler-laden sentences are frequently left as one piece even though leading connectives (그니까/그래서), trailing tag-questions, embedded question marks, and coordinating -고 clauses offer free, no-latency-cost boundaries. The secondary failure mode is wrong-boundary/over-segmentation where splits are placed right before a clause that still depends on the prior clause for its subject or causal connective, causing dropped subjects or hallucinated continuations.
